name: Diego Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the office on Station Road by half eight, before the phones start. Most of my clients are tenants facing eviction or people sacked without proper notice, and a lot of them are on legal aid, which is public money that pays for a lawyer when you can't. Mornings are calls and letters, afternoons are the county court or paperwork. I still print every file and write my notes by hand, which the others tease me about.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a family keeps their flat because a landlord got the notice wrong. You can see it on their faces. What wears me out is the pay and the billing targets. I'm on less than most lawyers my age, the rent on our flat keeps going up, and I've got less than a month's money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. People at work kept saying the firm would need clever software or be left behind, and I never believed it. Online I'd probably post that the money should have gone into legal aid instead of chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief, but it doesn't fix anything for me. My problems were never about AI. They're the rent, legal aid rates that haven't gone up in years, and the fact that there are maybe three firms in town doing my kind of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, the same files, the same court lists. I'd ask my boss again for the pay review she keeps pushing back, probably in January when the new rates come in. And I'd keep going to the housing lawyers' group that meets once a month at the community centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly flat, if I'm honest. Relieved the robots aren't coming for my desk, but still tired, still counting the days to payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned counting the days to payday. What does the last week of the month look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's pasta and the bus instead of the train. My partner works shifts as a care worker, and between us we cover the rent, but there's nothing left for anything going wrong. Last winter the boiler broke and we borrowed from her mum, which I hated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI only saves a bit of time here and there, would anyone at your firm use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trainee probably would, for first drafts of letters. I wouldn't touch it. A tenant's whole life is in that file, and I'm not handing it to something that makes things up.

say: I'd tell colleagues I **never believed** the firm needed clever software to survive.
Online I'd say the money should have gone into **legal aid**, not chatbots.
think: Privately it's a **relief**, but my real problems were never about AI.
The **rent**, frozen legal aid rates and only three local firms are what squeeze me.
do: Ask my boss again in January for the **pay review** she keeps delaying.
Keep the same files and court lists, and **refuse** to use AI for drafting.
Keep going to the monthly **housing lawyers' group** at the community centre.
feel: Mostly **flat**: relieved the robots aren't coming, but still tired and **counting days** to payday.
S0.quote: A tenant's whole life is in that file, and I'm not handing it to something that makes things up.
fieldNote: Money pressure, not technology, drives him; the **thin cushion** was there long before AI came up.
He already borrowed from his partner's mum to fix a **boiler**, and it still stings.
His refusal of AI is about **client trust**, not only habit.

steps.text: Ask the senior partner for the delayed pay review in January
Go to the monthly housing lawyers' group at the community centre

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster for ordinary people dressed up as progress. If a landlord's firm can churn out eviction notices with AI, tenants need more lawyers, not fewer. I'd be loud about it at the housing group and on the union's page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm exactly the kind of lawyer who gets squeezed. I'm average, I'm slow with tech, and half my day is writing letters and checking forms, which is exactly what AI takes first. The partners would look at me and the software bill and do the maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the lawyers' section of the union this month, which I've been meaning to do for a year. I'd start cutting back now: cancel the gym, stop eating out. And I'd try to get one month of rent saved by the summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like being told your skills have a sell-by date and nobody will say what it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom, our paralegal, first. He does the court bundles and the forms, and that's the first thing any software company would sell to my boss. Then me, to be honest, because I'm the one who still prints everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said tenants would need more lawyers, not fewer. Would that work protect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It should, but legal aid doesn't pay by need, it pays fixed fees. If the government decides AI can handle the easy cases, the fees drop and the firm takes fewer of them. So more need and less money for me, which is how it usually goes.

say: I'd call it a **disaster** for ordinary people, dressed up as progress.
I'd argue tenants facing AI-written eviction notices need **more lawyers**, not fewer.
think: I'm average, slow with tech and spend half my day on **letters and forms**.
The partners would weigh me against the **software bill** and do the maths.
do: Join the union's **lawyers' section** this month after a year of meaning to.
Cancel the gym and stop eating out **straight away**.
Save **one month of rent** by the summer.
feel: **Sick**, like his skills have a **sell-by date** nobody will name.
S1.quote: I'm average, I'm slow with tech, and half my day is writing letters and checking forms, which is exactly what AI takes first.
fieldNote: He sees himself, not just others, as **first in line** because he avoids software.
He worries for the **paralegal** before himself, which says a lot about him.
He knows legal aid pays **fixed fees**, so more need won't mean more income.

steps.text: Join the lawyers' section of the union this month
Cancel the gym and stop eating out
Save one month of rent by the summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need laws now: no AI giving legal advice without a human lawyer signing off, and a tax on the firms that profit. I'd be at every protest. I'd tell anyone who'd listen that justice can't be automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't think I'd have a job by 2029. Two years is nothing, and the robots coming three years later don't matter to me because nothing I do is hands-on. Maybe standing up in court lasts a bit longer, but that's an hour a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. I'd join the union and march, that's the one thing I know how to do. I'd ask my partner if we could move in with her mum to save the rent, and I'd look at retraining, but I have no money for a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panic, really. My chest goes tight. I spent five years and a mountain of student debt to get here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we might have to live on her wages for a while, and that's a care worker's wage. She'd say it's fine, because she always says that. Then I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say robots don't matter to you. Does the three-year gap help at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps my partner, not me. People will still need someone to lift and wash and sit with their dad for a few more years. My job is all in my head and on paper, so for me the clock starts in 2028, not 2031.

say: I'd demand a law that a **human lawyer** signs off any AI legal advice.
I'd go to every **protest** and say justice can't be automated.
think: I don't expect to **have a job** by 2029.
My work is all thinking, so the **robot delay** gives me nothing; maybe court lasts slightly longer.
do: Join the union and **march**, the one thing I know how to do.
Ask my partner about moving in with **her mum** to save rent.
Look at **retraining**, though I have no money for a course.
feel: **Panic** and a tight chest, thinking of **student debt** spent getting here.
S2.quote: My job is all in my head and on paper, so for me the clock starts in 2028, not 2031.
fieldNote: He has **no plan** beyond protest; the money to change course simply isn't there.
He sees clearly that his partner's **hands-on** care work outlasts his own job.
His public anger covers **private panic** about living on a care worker's wage.

steps.text: Join the union's lawyers' section and march for limits on AI advice
Lobby for a law requiring a human lawyer to sign off advice
Ask his partner's mum about moving in to save the rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as before, just with more time to organise. I'd want the unions and the law society pushing for rules before 2031, not after. Five years is enough for a proper campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years buys me some runway but not a career. I'd be 32 when it lands and still have no savings unless something changes. The court work and sitting with frightened clients might last a little longer than the letters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving properly, even fifty a month, into an account I can't see. In the first two years I'd try to get more court work, so I'm the one who stands up, not the one who drafts. And I'd look at jobs with the union's legal team, because if anyone keeps people around, it's a union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less frozen than the fast one. It's like seeing a storm on the horizon instead of having it on top of you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned being 32 when it lands. Would this change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would. My partner and I talk about kids around thirty, and I'd want to wait and see where we stood. I don't want to bring a child into a flat we can't pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn to use AI tools in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably only if I'm forced to. I know that sounds stubborn. But I've seen a tool invent a court case on the news, and I'd rather be the person who checks the machine than the one who trusts it.

say: I'd push unions and the law society for **rules before 2031**, not after.
I'd say five years is enough for a **proper campaign**.
think: Five years buys **runway**, not a career, and I'd still have no savings.
**Court work** and frightened clients might outlast the letters for a while.
do: Save **fifty a month** into an account I can't see.
Ask for more **court work** in the first two years.
Apply for jobs with the **union's legal team**.
feel: **Worried** but less frozen, like a **storm** on the horizon.
S3.quote: I don't want to bring a child into a flat we can't pay for.
fieldNote: The extra time turns his panic into a **rough plan**, though still a worried one.
He would delay **children** until he knows where he stands.
He'd rather **check the machine** than use it, and admits that sounds stubborn.

steps.text: Save fifty a month into a separate account
Apply for a role on the union's legal team
Wait on having children until his income is clear
Campaign with the unions for AI rules before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if governments actually use it. Plan the retraining, fund legal aid properly, decide now who signs off on machine advice. If they waste it, that's on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is different. I'd be 37, and I could change direction once instead of being thrown. The worry doesn't go, though, because I've watched governments waste ten years on housing already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give myself two years to look properly at a move into a union or a tenants' advice charity. I'd pay off my credit card first, then build three months of savings. And I'd push the partners for a written policy on AI so they can't quietly replace people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but breathing. It's the only one of the three where I feel like I'm holding the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first to build those three months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, honestly. It's an old hatchback that costs more in repairs than it's worth, and the bus gets me to the office. That's two hundred a month back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You trust governments to use the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not really. That's the contradiction, I know. I'd campaign as if governments will use it and save as if they won't.

say: I'd call ten years a **gift**, if governments actually use it.
I'd want **legal aid** funded and sign-off rules for machine advice decided now.
think: At 37 I could **change direction** once instead of being thrown.
I've watched governments **waste ten years** on housing already.
do: Look at a move to a union or **tenants' charity** within two years.
Clear the **credit card**, then build three months of savings.
Push the partners for a **written AI policy**.
feel: **Uneasy but breathing**, the only picture where he holds the wheel.
S4.quote: I'd campaign as if governments will use it and save as if they won't.
fieldNote: A decade gives him a sense of **control** the faster pictures don't.
He names his own **contradiction**: campaigning for governments he doesn't trust.
Selling the **old hatchback** is his first concrete saving.

steps.text: Sell the old hatchback and take the bus to work
Pay off the credit card, then save three months
Apply within two years to a tenants' advice charity
Push the partners to agree a written AI policy

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. Two years with no savings and a job that's all paperwork is a cliff. What would help is a rule that a human lawyer has to stand behind legal advice, and paid retraining so people like me aren't choosing between a course and the rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the clients. Everyone talks about lawyers losing jobs, but my clients are the ones who'll be stuck arguing with a machine about their eviction. Nobody's asking them.

headlineQuote: My clients are the ones who'll be stuck arguing with a machine about their eviction.
portrait: Diego is a **27-year-old** tenant and employment lawyer at a small firm, paid less than most peers.
He has **under a month** saved, rents with his partner, a care worker, and never uses AI.
In the milder pictures his worry is **money**, not machines; frozen legal aid rates already squeeze him.
The fast AGI picture leaves him **panicked**, because nearly all his work is thinking and paperwork.
With a decade he would **campaign and save**, aiming for union or tenants' charity work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**: two years, no savings and a job made of **paperwork**.
whatWouldHelp: A rule that a **human lawyer** must stand behind legal advice.
**Paid retraining**, so he isn't choosing between a course and the rent.
